summary: Slovakia is a landlocked country in Central Europe with natural landscapes such as the Tatra Mountains; it became independent in 1993 after a peaceful separation from the Czech Republic.

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: In 863 the brothers Cyril and Methodius came at the invitation of Great Moravia to preach, and Christianity took root in Slovakia; from the 11th century the area was incorporated into the Catholic Kingdom of Hungary. The 16th-century Reformation briefly made Protestantism prevalent, but in the 17th century the Habsburg dynasty pushed the Counter-Reformation, which brought most people back to Catholicism. From 1948 to 1989 the communist regime closed monasteries and persecuted clergy, and the 1988 "Candle Demonstration" in Bratislava became a harbinger of the anti-communist movement, so Catholicism is still closely tied to Slovak national identity and is especially devout in the northern and eastern countryside.

ranking.name: No religion
ranking.description: After the communists took power in 1948 they pursued atheist education, church property was confiscated and religious activity was monitored, so many families stopped having their children baptized. After the Velvet Revolution of 1989 religious freedom was restored, but urbanization and secularization among the younger generation have kept increasing the number of people with no religion, whose share rose markedly in the 2021 census, mainly in cities such as the capital, Bratislava.

ranking.name: Lutheranism
ranking.description: Luther's 16th-century Reformation arrived through the inhabitants of German mining towns and then spread among the Slovaks, who long used the Czech-language Kralice Bible. After the 17th-century Counter-Reformation the Protestants became a minority, but leaders of the 19th-century Slovak national revival such as Ľudovít Štúr came from Lutheran families, so this denomination has had a far greater influence on cultural history than its numbers suggest.

ranking.name: Greek Catholicism
ranking.description: In the 1646 Union of Uzhhorod, Orthodox clergy in the east, such as the Rusyns, acknowledged the authority of the Roman pope while keeping the Byzantine rite, forming the Greek Catholic Church. In 1950 the communist regime forced this church to merge into the Orthodox Church, and it was not made legal again until the Prague Spring in 1968. Its believers are mainly the Rusyns and Slovaks around Prešov in the east.

religion.background: In the 9th century, during the Great Moravian period, the mission of Cyril and Methodius brought Christianity to Slovakia. For almost a thousand years afterward Slovakia belonged to the Kingdom of Hungary; the 16th-century Reformation brought Lutheranism, and the Habsburg Counter-Reformation of the 17th century made Catholicism the majority again. In the east the Greek Catholic Church formed in 1646. From 1948 to 1989 communist rule severely suppressed religion, and after 1989 religious freedom was restored; Catholicism remains the mainstream, but the number of people with no religion is growing year by year.

ranking.name: Slovak
ranking.description: Slovak belongs to the West Slavic branch and is highly mutually intelligible with Czech. Under the Kingdom of Hungary, Latin, German and Hungarian were long the languages of administration; in 1787 Anton Bernolák first codified a written Slovak, and in 1843 Ľudovít Štúr built today's standard language on the central dialect. After 1867 Hungary pursued a policy of Magyarization that suppressed Slovak, and it did not become an official language until the founding of Czechoslovakia in 1918; after independence in 1993 it is the sole national language, and most citizens have it as their mother tongue.

ranking.name: Hungarian
ranking.description: Hungarian speakers are concentrated in the southern regions bordering Hungary, such as Komárno and Dunajská Streda. When the 1920 Treaty of Trianon drew the borders, these areas with a Hungarian majority were assigned to Czechoslovakia, forming today's Hungarian minority. Although there were population exchanges and expulsions after World War II, a large number of Hungarians remained, and to this day they have Hungarian-language schools, newspapers and local official-language status.

ranking.name: Romani
ranking.description: The ancestors of the Roma originated in northern India and had appeared in the Slovak area by around the 15th century; they live mainly in the east and south, many in impoverished settlements. Because of discrimination and pressure to assimilate, many Roma register as Slovaks or Hungarians in the census, so the number who actually speak Romani should be higher than the statistics.

language.history: Slovak belongs to the West Slavic branch; in the Middle Ages the written and religious language of the area was Latin, and after the Reformation Czech was also widely used. At the end of the 18th century Bernolák first wrote the western dialect as a standard language, and in the mid-19th century Štúr instead established a written language on the central dialect, which became a symbol of the national revival movement. In the late 19th century Hungary pursued Magyarization and Slovak-language schools were closed; after Czechoslovakia was founded in 1918 the status of the language rose, and after independence in 1993 it became the sole national language.

ranking.name: Bryndzové halušky (sheep cheese dumplings)
ranking.description: Small dumplings made of raw grated potato and flour, boiled and tossed with bryndza sheep cheese and sprinkled with crisply fried bacon bits, rich and slightly salty.
ranking.history: The so-called "Wallachian colonization" of the 14th–17th centuries brought the shepherding traditions of the Carpathians into the Slovak mountains, so sheep cheese became the main source of protein for mountain dwellers. Potatoes became common there only in the 18th century, and shepherds and farmers combined cheap potato dumplings with sheep cheese to form this filling mountain dish. Today it is widely recognized as the national dish of Slovakia, and dumpling-eating contests and festivals are held in many places.

ranking.name: Kapustnica (sauerkraut soup)
ranking.description: A thick soup made from pickled sauerkraut simmered for a long time with smoked sausage, pork, dried mushrooms and prunes, sour with a smoky aroma.
ranking.history: With few vegetables available in winter, Central European farm families pickled large amounts of cabbage into sauerkraut in autumn to preserve it, so kapustnica became the most common winter soup. Its most important moment in Slovakia is Christmas Eve dinner: Catholic tradition requires fasting before Christmas Eve, and at dinner a bowl of sauerkraut soup is drunk before the fried carp, symbolizing the start of the festival. Methods vary from place to place, with dried mushrooms and prunes often added in the west and a white version with cream in the east.

ranking.name: Pirohy (dumplings)
ranking.description: Half-moon-shaped dumplings of dough filled with mashed potato, bryndza sheep cheese or plum jam, boiled and topped with butter or fried onion.
ranking.history: Dumplings of this kind are common throughout the Slavic lands, including Poland, Ukraine and Slovakia, and their names all derive from an Old Slavic word meaning "pie, feast." In Slovakia pirohy are especially popular in the east, which is influenced by Rusyn and Ukrainian culture, and are often filled with the potatoes and sheep cheese the area produces in abundance. In the past they were commonly eaten by farm families on festival days and fast days (days without meat), and both sweet and savory versions exist.

ranking.name: Lokše (potato flatbread)
ranking.description: Mashed potato kneaded with flour into a dough, rolled out into thin flatbreads and cooked on a dry pan or stovetop, then spread with goose fat or wrapped around poppy seeds or jam.
ranking.history: Lokše are a traditional flatbread of the western countryside that appeared only after potatoes became common in the 18th century, turning leftover potatoes into a cheap staple. The most famous way to eat them is in the village of Slovenský Grob near Bratislava, served with roast goose and goose fat, where a "goose festival" is held every autumn, close in time to St. Martin's Day in November. Eating goose on St. Martin's Day is a Central European Catholic custom, so lokše have become a symbol of autumn festivals.

ranking.name: Bryndza (sheep cheese)
ranking.description: A soft cheese made from sheep's milk, aged and salted, with a smooth, spreadable texture and a salty, slightly sour taste, which can be spread on bread, mixed into dumplings or used as a dumpling filling.
ranking.history: The bryndza tradition comes from the Wallachian shepherds who moved into the Slovak mountains in the 14th–17th centuries and made sheep's milk into cheese that could be kept. In 1787 the first bryndza dairy appeared in Detva in central Slovakia, turning it from a shepherds' home-made food into a commodity that could be sold. In 2008 "Slovenská bryndza" obtained EU protected geographical indication, and it is the indispensable star of the national dish, bryndzové halušky.
